evidence.claim: Down in the Little Tennessee Valley, an earlier transformation began in 1909, when Alcoa started developing hydroelectric power for its aluminum smelters in Blount County.
evidence.quote: Alcoa began developing the Little Tennessee Valley in 1909 to provide the enormous amounts of electricity needed to power to its aluminum smelting operations in Blount County.

evidence.claim: The camp was established in 1912 and initially called Alcoa; in 1920 it was renamed for engineer I. G. Calderwood, who led the company’s work in the valley.
evidence.quote: In 1912, a post office was set up in the base camp, which initially used the company's name, "Alcoa."

evidence.claim: The camp was established in 1912 and initially called Alcoa; in 1920 it was renamed for engineer I. G. Calderwood, who led the company’s work in the valley.
evidence.quote: The following year, the company renamed its Little Tennessee Valley construction camp "Calderwood" after its able head of operations in the valley, I. G. Calderwood.

evidence.claim: Begin at Deals Gap on the North Carolina-Tennessee line, then follow US 129 into Tennessee through the Dragon’s bends.
evidence.quote: The area is popular with motorcycle and sports car enthusiasts, who cross the gap into Tennessee to drive along the "Tail of the Dragon"

evidence.claim: Calderwood Overlook stands beside US 129 just south of Housley Road, with a view across the reservoir.
evidence.quote: The Calderwood Overlook, located along US-129 just south of the road's intersection with Housley Road, provides a sweeping view of the Calderwood Reservoir.

evidence.claim: Housley Road leads down to the surviving Calderwood community buildings on the riverfront.
evidence.quote: The surviving community structures and the Calderwood Dam service building are accessible via Housley Road, which connects US-129 with Growdon Road on the riverfront.

evidence.claim: At 1,988 feet, Deals Gap marks the mountain crossing on the North Carolina-Tennessee line beside Great Smoky Mountains National Park.
evidence.quote: Deals Gap (el. 1,988 ft (606 m)) is a mountain pass along the North Carolina–Tennessee state line, bordering the Great Smoky Mountains National Park

evidence.claim: The community with the same name lies 0.7 miles south, at US 129 and NC 28.
evidence.quote: At 0.7 miles (1.1 km) south of the gap is the unincorporated community that shares the same name, located at the intersection of US 129 and NC 28.

evidence.claim: Alcoa built Calderwood as one of four dams supplying electricity to its aluminum smelting operations in Blount County.
evidence.quote: Calderwood Dam was one of four dams—along with Cheoah, Santeetlah, and Chilhowee—built in the Little Tennessee Valley by Alcoa in the 20th century to provide electricity to its aluminum smelting operations in Blount County.

evidence.claim: The engineering uses a horseshoe bend called the Narrows: the dam occupies the upstream end, while the powerhouse sits downstream.
evidence.quote: The Calderwood complex graces a horseshoe bend in the river known as "The Narrows." The dam is located along the upstream end of this bend, and the powerhouse, service building, and old Calderwood community (now a recreation area) are located along the downstream end of this bend.

evidence.claim: A 2,150-foot concrete tunnel carries diverted river water through the peninsula toward the generating equipment.
evidence.quote: A submerged intake just upstream from the dam diverts water into a 2,150-foot (660 m) concrete tunnel, which carries the water to the other side of the peninsula

evidence.claim: A smaller dam below the main structure creates a cushion pool that protects the riverbed; the design drew on the action of natural cascades.
evidence.quote: A 40-foot (12 m) lower-gravity "cushion" dam is located 370 feet (110 m) downstream from the main dam, creating a pool of water that protects the riverbed.

evidence.claim: A smaller dam below the main structure creates a cushion pool that protects the riverbed; the design drew on the action of natural cascades.
evidence.quote: The "cushion pool" design of Calderwood was influenced by natural cascade waterfall formations.

evidence.claim: The reservoir lies below the US 129 overlook.
evidence.quote: provides a sweeping view of the Calderwood Reservoir.

evidence.claim: The gravel road from the overlook to Calderwood Dam is open only to public foot traffic.
evidence.quote: A gravel road, also open only to public foot traffic, connects the overlook to Calderwood Dam.

evidence.claim: A school and a Quonset-hut theater survive where dam workers once lived.
evidence.quote: Although the community's houses were razed after its abandonment, three buildings located in the community— the Calderwood Dam service building, the Calderwood School, and a Quonset hut used as a theater— were included in a supplementary listing

evidence.claim: Alcoa established the settlement in 1912 as a base for its Little Tennessee Valley hydroelectric projects.
evidence.quote: Established in 1912 as a base for the Aluminum Company of America's Little Tennessee Valley hydroelectric development operations

evidence.claim: After Calderwood Dam’s completion, maintenance crews replaced construction crews, and the community gained a school and theater in 1950.
evidence.quote: In 1950, a school was built, and a Quonset hut was installed in the community for use as a theater.

evidence.claim: After Calderwood Dam’s completion, maintenance crews replaced construction crews, and the community gained a school and theater in 1950.
evidence.quote: After the completion of Calderwood Dam in 1930, the construction camp evolved into a community that housed maintenance crews for the dam.

evidence.claim: As the need for onsite crews diminished, residents moved away.
evidence.quote: Within a few years, the need for onsite crews diminished, however, and residents began moving away.

evidence.claim: The houses were demolished; their foundations and two garages remain alongside the surviving community buildings.
evidence.quote: The residences in the community have all been razed, and only their foundations and two garages remain.

evidence.claim: The Methodist church remains intact, while the Baptist church has partly collapsed, leaving its front facade. Neither church was included in the dam’s National Register listing.
evidence.quote: The Calderwood Methodist Church is still intact, but the Calderwood Baptist Church has partially collapsed (the front facade remains).  Neither church was included in the National Register listing.

evidence.claim: Housley Road, the access road to the community structures, is gated at night.
evidence.quote: The service building, recreation area, and historical community structures are accessible via Housley Road (gated at night)
